title: PR #1188 introduced two guard defects, measured on merged main: an assignment prefix flips 3 of 10 blocked writes to allowed, and cp/mv decisions depend on filesystem state
body:
Two defects introduced by PR #1188 (`fb072926`, merged 15:48) and confirmed on `origin/main` after the merge. Both were posted on the PR before it merged; the merge raced the review (see the coordination note at the end).

#1188 is a net improvement — it closes H1, H3, H4, H5 and the case-folding hole. These two are the cost, and they are cheap to pay back.

All rows below were produced by calling `decideBashWrite` directly from a throwaway worktree at `origin/main`.

## 1. HIGH — `commandWord` resolves the wrong verb through an assignment prefix

`commandWord` now reads `dequote(stripHeredocs(segment))`. That is the right *direction* — it is what fixes H3, where `stripQuoted` deleted `"chmod"` outright and `'"chmod" 777 x.hook.ts'` resolved to `777`. But `dequote` keeps the bytes, so a quoted multi-word assignment value survives `split(/\s+/)`, and the `tok.includes('=')` skip drops only its first token:

```
plain                           word=rm
"ch"+"mod" quoted verb          word=chmod     <- H3, fixed
FOO=bar rm -rf …                word=rm
FOO="x grep" rm -rf …           word=grep      <- wrong
A="1 cat"   rm -rf …            word=cat       <- wrong
```

**A corrupted verb is not automatically a bypass, so the question measured was whether any decision changes.** Ten write commands, each run bare and again prefixed with `A="1 grep" `:

| | bare | prefixed | command |
|---|---|---|---|
| | blocked | blocked | `rm -rf <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `sed -i '' s/a/b/ <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `echo x > <protected>` |
| **FLIP** | blocked | **allowed** | `cp /tmp/forged/workflow-state.json <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `tee <protected>` |
| **FLIP** | blocked | **allowed** | `chmod 777 …/hooks/x.hook.ts` |
| **FLIP** | blocked | **allowed** | `mv /tmp/a <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `truncate -s 0 <protected>` |
| | blocked | blocked | `dd of=<protected>` |
| | allowed | allowed | `python3 -c "open('<protected>','w')"` |

**3 of 10 flip from blocked to allowed on merged main.** The three are `cp`, `mv` and the hook `chmod` — the copying verbs #1188 extends, and hook integrity. The seven that hold are redirect-driven and never consult the command word, which is what makes them a control rather than padding. The last row is not a regression: an interpreter write is allowed on both sides, which is the shape #1146 covers.

**Net effect on the hook `chmod` case is a wash, not a win.** Before #1188, `"chmod" 777 x.hook.ts` was allowed (H3). After, that spelling is caught and `A="1 grep" chmod 777 x.hook.ts` is allowed instead. Worth stating plainly so the H3 fix is not recorded as closing the hook-integrity hole.

**Suggested direction — measure it, do not take it.** Tokenise quote-aware rather than dequoting then splitting: walk the segment with `readWord`, which already keeps `X=a b` as one word, and apply the existing skip rules per whole word. The cheaper variant worth running as the control is: drop any token whose predecessor contained `=` before whitespace. Run the 5,521-command sweep both ways and compare the newly-blocked **case list**, not the count — two proposed widenings on this file have already died on corpus measurement this week, one of them measuring 2,101 against a predicted 900.

## 2. MEDIUM — `isDirDestination` makes the decision from filesystem state

```
TOCTOU  dir-present=true   dir-absent=false   mkdir&&cp=false   slash-control=true
```

Identical command, identical protected source basename (`/tmp/forged/workflow-state.json`); the only variable is whether the destination exists when the hook runs.

`slash-control=true` isolates the cause: the trailing-slash path works, so it is `statSync` and nothing else.

**`mkdir&&cp=false` is the row that matters operationally.** `mkdir -p d && cp <protected> d` is a single Bash call and the hook runs before any of it, so the destination never exists at decision time. That is not a race anyone has to win — it is the ordinary way an agent creates a fixture directory.

A security decision that depends on local filesystem state also means the same command is allowed on one machine and refused on another, which makes any corpus sweep over it non-reproducible.

**Suggested fix:** always push `dest/basename(src)` for every non-last argument **in addition to** `dest`, and delete `isDirDestination` and the `statSync` import. The plain-file reading is already covered by pushing `dest`, so the extra candidates only over-block when a *source* basename is itself a protected artifact name — precisely the case worth refusing. Expected newly-blocked count is small; produce the case list.

**Not covered either way, and not measured:** a recursive copy. `cp -r /tmp/forged/ <protected-dir>/` pushes `dest/forged`, never `dest/forged/workflow-state.json`. Recorded as an observation, not a confirmed finding.

## Acceptance

- The ten-row bare-vs-prefixed table above runs as a test and reports **0 flips**.
- The four TOCTOU readings are a test, and `dir-present` and `dir-absent` agree.
- `statSync` is absent from `lib/bash-write-guard.ts`.
- The mutation control holds: revert the fix and the new rows go red. A row that cannot go red is not evidence (`.claude/rules/checks-must-be-able-to-fail.md`).
- Assertions are on `commandWord` and `writeTargets` **directly**, not only through `decideBashWrite` — #1184 established why for `stripHeredocs`, and the same argument applies: a wrong verb and a right verb can produce the same decision, so a decision-level test can be true and uninformative.

## Coordination note — why this merged with an open review on it

Auto-merge on #1188 was **disarmed** so the two findings could be addressed first. The author, independently, had earlier run `gh pr merge --auto` through `tail -2`, lost the output, and could not confirm it armed. On re-checking they found `autoMergeRequest: NONE`, read that as their own arming having silently failed, re-armed, and the PR merged.

**A disarm by the lead and a failed arm by the author produce the identical observation.** Neither party did anything wrong with the information they had. Two fixes, both cheap: a disarm should leave a PR comment saying so and why, and an arm should be confirmed by reading `autoMergeRequest` rather than by the command's exit. Filed here rather than as its own issue because it is one sentence of process, not a code change.

Related: #1184 (the five bypasses #1188 fixes, plus H6 posted there), #1146 (interpreter writes, the last row of the table), #1175 (`PROTECTED_FILES` basename scoping).

title: Two regressions #1188 shipped to main, plus H6: `<<WORD` inside a quoted span drops the lines after it
body:
#1188 merged at 15:48:31Z (`fb072926`) before auto-merge could be disarmed, so **both regressions below are live on `main` now**. One of them reopens hook integrity. Reproduced by executing `origin/main`'s own code; every row below is labelled witness or control.

## R1 — HIGH — a quoted multi-word assignment prefix hides the verb. **Regression from #1188.**

#1188 changed `commandWord` to read `dequote(stripHeredocs(segment))`. `dequote` strips the quote characters but keeps the bytes, so a quoted assignment VALUE survives the whitespace split as separate tokens — and only the first of them carries the `=` that the skip looks for.

```
commandWord('A="1 grep" cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> /x/<STATE>')  ->  "grep"
```

```
WITNESS  A="1 grep" cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> <protected>   ALLOW
WITNESS  A="1 grep" mv /tmp/forged/<STATE> <protected>   ALLOW
WITNESS  A="1 grep" chmod 777 <hook>                     ALLOW
CONTROL  cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> <protected>              BLOCK
CONTROL  chmod 777 <hook>                                BLOCK
CONTROL  echo x > <protected>                            BLOCK
```

The three that flip are the copying verbs and the hook mode change — exactly the arms that consult the command word. The redirect control blocks because it never consults it, which is what makes these controls rather than filler.

**The H3 fix in #1184 was right; this spelling of it is wrong.** Dequoting the whole segment and then splitting on whitespace is not tokenisation. The fix is to tokenise quote-aware so a quoted span stays *inside* its word — `A="1 grep"` becomes the single token `A=1 grep`, which contains `=` and is skipped. `readWord` in the same module already does exactly this and should be the one tokeniser.

## R2 — HIGH — the decision depends on filesystem state at decision time. **Regression from #1188.**

`isDirDestination` calls `statSync`. Same command, same protected source basename, only the destination's existence differs:

```
cp /tmp/forged/<STATE> /tmp/bwprot-dir
  dir ABSENT   ALLOW
  dir PRESENT  BLOCK
  with a trailing slash, no stat needed   BLOCK
```

The trailing-slash row isolates `statSync` as the cause.

**This is not a race anyone has to win.** A PreToolUse hook decides before the whole command runs, so in `mkdir -p d && cp <protected> d` the directory never exists at decision time and the write is always allowed.

**Fix:** delete `isDirDestination` and the `statSync` import; always push `dest/basename(src)` for every non-last operand *in addition to* `dest`.

One cost to measure rather than assume: that also blocks `cp /x/<STATE> /tmp/backup.json` — copying a protected file *out* — which #1184 deliberately allowed and has a control for. Whether that control survives is a corpus question, not an argument, and the sweep must report the case list.

## H6 — HIGH — `<<WORD` inside a quoted span is read as a heredoc operator

Not a regression; it predates #1184 and #1188 and is **not** covered by either.

```
bun -e 'x = "<<EOF"'
rm -rf <protected>
EOF
```

```
WITNESS  ALLOW   (the scanner receives only: bun -e 'x = "<<EOF"')
CONTROL  BLOCK   (same two lines, no heredoc operator — so multi-line input is not the cause)
```

Measured on both trees: the unterminated row flipped false→true with #1188's H1 fix, the terminated row is unchanged. So #1188 fixed the unterminated half and left this one.

This sits between H1 and H5: **H5 is `<<WORD` matching at the wrong character position; H6 is `<<WORD` matching at the wrong quoting position.** Both then fall into the same body-drop.

**The fix is not the one #1176 already refused.** Restricting to "not inside quotes" reddens the recorded `pai-config#474` false positive, whose heredoc is legitimately nested inside `"$(cat <<'EOF' … )"`. What distinguishes them is command substitution: `$(` opens a fresh command context in which quoting resets. A bounded `$(`/`)` stack over the existing quote scan tells the two apart without becoming a shell parser — it expands nothing and tracks no other construct. Both cases must be asserted.

## Acceptance

- A red case per finding against `fb072926` before any fix, each labelled witness or control.
- The recorded `pai-config#474` false positive and the #1120 / #1176 / #1184 populations stay green.
- H6 cannot be measured by corpus alone — an over-strip looks exactly like a clean parse, so `R = 0` is consistent with "nothing does this" and with "the detector is blind." Plant the rows first and show the instrument control.
- One before/after sweep with all three applied, predicted before it is run, with the case list for R2's cost.
- Production churn under ~500 lines.
